summary: This unit teaches you to plan and lead the negotiation of an important public-sector purchase. You will learn to place a purchase on the supply positioning (Kraljic) matrix, judge the market, work out total cost of ownership, plan aims, limits and concessions, organise a negotiating team, conduct the talks fairly within the procurement rules, handle pressure tactics, negotiate non-price terms, record and approve the agreement, and manage the supplier afterwards.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. Public bodies in Jamaica (ministries, agencies, hospitals, schools and municipal corporations) spend large sums on goods, works and services. For the most important purchases, a manager must do more than accept the lowest bid: she must plan and conduct a **negotiation** that gets good value, keeps the process fair and builds a workable relationship with the supplier.

**Procurement** is the whole process of buying: deciding the need, finding suppliers, evaluating offers, awarding the contract and managing it. **Strategic procurement** deals with purchases that are high in value or impact, long in duration or hard to replace, for example a five-year contract to supply and maintain medical equipment, a network maintenance contract or a multi-year cleaning contract for a hospital. These need more planning, more people and more care.

Public money must be spent with **fairness, openness and value for money**. Negotiation in the public sector is therefore different from a private deal: you may negotiate **only as the procurement rules and the tender documents allow**, you must treat bidders equally, you must keep bids confidential, and you must be able to show an auditor that the process was honest.
**Who it is for:** supervisors, officers and managers in public bodies who are given a procurement negotiation to plan or lead, or who sit on a negotiating team.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Analyse the purchase and the market
Place the purchase on the supply positioning matrix, judge supplier power, and know what the item really costs over its life.
Work within the rules and probity standards
Negotiate only what the rules and tender documents allow, declare conflicts, refuse gifts and keep confidences.
Agree aims, priorities, limits, walk-away point, concessions, team roles, authority and agenda in a written plan.
Compare total cost of ownership, discounts, early-payment terms and warranties, and check every sum twice.
Open clearly, explore interests, trade concessions, handle pressure tactics and deadlock, and summarise.
Secure service levels, remedies, price adjustment, warranty and exit terms that protect the body.
Write up what was agreed, confirm it, get approval, and keep full records.
Run the relationship after signing, and hold a debrief to learn lessons.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions, including percentage, discount and total-cost sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as total cost of ownership, Kraljic matrix, concession) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Group practical tasks**: plan a negotiation from a pack, then conduct a role-play negotiation with a supplier team and record the agreement. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, by two different routes. A wrong figure in a negotiation costs money, and a wrong figure in the record can be an audit finding.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The rules, probity and your authority

blocks.p: The **procurement rules for public bodies in Jamaica** aim at **value for money through fair, open buying**. In general terms they require public bodies to buy competitively and transparently, to treat suppliers equally, to follow set steps and thresholds, to keep records and to account for public money. Learn the rules your own body works under and ask your procurement officer when in doubt.

blocks.h: May we negotiate after a tender?

blocks.p: After tenders are evaluated, the body may talk with the **preferred bidder** (the bidder ranked first after evaluation) **only as the rules and the tender documents allow, and fairly**. Negotiation is normally about how the preferred bid is delivered and agreed (clarifications, terms, delivery, payment, warranty, service levels), not a chance to rewrite the tender.

head: Situation
What it means
rows: The tender documents say that negotiation on named matters is allowed
Changing scope, quantity or specification greatly
Other bidders might have bid differently; consider re-tendering, because fairness is affected
Asking the preferred bidder to match another bidder's price
Not allowed: other bids are confidential
Negotiating something the documents and rules do not allow
Do not; seek advice from the procurement officer and legal adviser first

blocks.p: **Probity** means honest, fair and open conduct that lets a procurement stand up to scrutiny. The key rules are below.

head: Rule
In practice
rows: Every team member signs a declaration before talks begin; anyone with a private interest steps aside
Politely decline and record the offer; report it under the code of conduct
Never reveal other bidders' prices or the agency's maximum price; keep the team's limits within the team
Never invent a competing offer or give false facts
Give all bidders the same information and chances
If you receive information you should not have, do not use it and report it
Keep a full record so the process can be audited

blocks.p: Officers can commit public money only up to the limit of the **delegation** (formal authority) given to them. If the supplier offers a deal that is good value but above the lead negotiator's limit, she should say she must **seek approval** before agreeing, and then do so. The final contract must be signed by an **officer with authority for that value**.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, public procurement is governed by legislation and by policies issued by the national procurement authorities. Refer to the procurement rules and your body's procurement officer for thresholds, approvals and permitted negotiation. Do not rely on memory for limits or procedures.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Analysing the purchase and the market

blocks.p: The **Kraljic matrix** sorts purchases by two things: the **cost or impact** of the purchase on the body, and the **supply risk** (how few suppliers can provide it, how hard it is to switch). It shows what approach to use.

head: Category
Cost / impact
Supply risk
Example
Approach
rows: Simplify; use standard terms and catalogues; spend little time
Large amounts of office paper, fuel
Use competition and volume to get the best price
A spare part only one firm stocks
Secure supply; keep stock; look for alternatives
Five-year imaging equipment contract; specialised radio network maintenance
Plan carefully; build a long-term relationship; negotiate fully

blocks.p: Strategic items matter most. A five-year imaging equipment supply contract in a public hospital is strategic procurement: it is expensive, long, hard to replace and affects patient care.

Ask: how many suppliers can do this? How easily can we switch? How badly do they need our business? If only two firms in Jamaica can maintain a ministry's specialised radio network, **supplier power is high** and the body's bargaining power is lower. Prepare especially carefully, look for alternatives, and avoid showing urgency. If many suppliers compete, the buyer has **bargaining power**.

head: Factor
Raises the buyer's power
Raises the supplier's power
rows: Supplier knows more than the buyer

blocks.p: **Total cost of ownership (TCO)** is the full cost of an item over its life: purchase price, running costs, maintenance, training and disposal. The cheapest price at purchase is not always the cheapest overall.

**Should-cost estimate:** the buyer's estimate of what the item should fairly cost, built up by parts (materials, labour, overheads, margin). It helps you judge whether a supplier's price is reasonable.
**Evidence for a renewal:** past performance, cost and complaint records of the existing supplier are the most useful source when preparing to negotiate a contract renewal.

blocks.note: Never negotiate on price alone. A cheap purchase price with high servicing costs, long delays or poor quality can cost far more than a fairer price with strong terms.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A negotiation is won or lost before the first meeting. Prepare a **written negotiation plan**.

flow: Confirm what the rules and tender documents allow you to negotiate
Agree the team's aims in order of priority
Work out the figures: budget, should-cost, total cost, the offer on the table
Set the limits: target, opening position and walk-away point
List possible concessions and what each is worth to each side
Assign roles and confirm authority and communication rules
Prepare the agenda, the evidence and the questions to ask
Rehearse, including how to handle pressure

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: What the body wants from the deal, in priority order
1. Price within budget. 2. Service levels with measures. 3. Faster delivery
The outcome you hope to reach
Where you start; sets an anchor
The worst deal you will accept; set before talks and never shown to the supplier
J$75 million: no worse than the best alternative, and within authority
What you will do if talks fail, such as turning to the next-ranked bidder or re-tendering

blocks.p: Fix the walk-away point **before** talks, so the team never accepts worse than its best alternative under pressure. It must fit the **budget** and the **authority** the team has.

Price is only one of the things you can negotiate. Within the rules, a public buyer can usually negotiate **delivery dates, payment terms, training, warranty, service levels, contract length, price adjustment, reporting and other terms**.

List items that cost you little but that the supplier values highly (for example a longer contract, quicker payment or clear forecasts of volume) and items that the supplier could give cheaply but you value highly (training, warranty). Plan to **trade** them.

head: Role
What the person does
rows: Speaks for the team, controls the pace and keeps to the plan and to authority limits
Answers specification and quality questions (for an ICT system, ICT staff)
Checks figures, total cost and payment terms
Logs offers, concessions and agreements as they happen
Watches the supplier's behaviour and the team's discipline

blocks.p: A contract for a new ICT system for a ministry needs procurement, ICT, finance and legal staff. **Agree who may speak, signals for a break, and how the team communicates privately during the talks.** Every team member signs the conflict of interest declaration. Keep the team's limits within the team.
**Written plan contents:** aims, limits, concessions, roles and agenda.
Check every figure twice. Below are the sums you will meet.

head: Sum
Method
Worked example
rows: Total cost of ownership over n years
Work TCO for each over the same years
(first offer - agreed price) / first offer x 100
Compare extra price with repair costs avoided
Extra J$900,000 against repairs of J$600,000 a year in years 2 and 3 = J$1,200,000: saves J$300,000

blocks.p: Discounts linked to a **condition** (a longer contract, a bigger order, faster payment, lower service level) must be tested. Ask: what do we give up, what is the real saving, can we use what we are asked to buy, and is the change allowed under the rules?

Worked example: a supplier offers 8% off a J$25,000,000 contract if the agency commits to three years instead of two. The saving on J$25,000,000 is J$2,000,000. But the third year also adds spending and commitment; compare like with like (total over the same period) and check that the supplier's performance justifies a longer commitment.

blocks.note: Percentage of what? A saving is usually stated against the budget or the first offer. Say which. A 10% reduction from J$48 million is J$4.8 million; the same J$4.8 million is a different percentage of a J$60 million budget.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Percentage fall:** a price cut from J$20,000,000 to J$18,500,000 is a fall of 1,500,000 / 20,000,000 = 7.5%. **Percentage of budget spent:** J$5,200,000 of J$8,000,000 is 65%.

flow: Open: introduce the team, confirm the purpose, agenda, time and authority
Explore: ask questions to learn the supplier's interests and constraints
Propose: present your position with reasons and evidence
Bargain: trade concessions, one condition for another
Summarise: confirm each agreed point as you go
Close: record what was agreed and what happens next

blocks.p: A **position** is what someone says they want ('payment in 15 days'). An **interest** is why ('we need cash flow for materials'). If the supplier insists on payment within 15 days but the agency's system pays in 30, **ask why it needs quick payment, then explore options**: staged payments, an invoice discount for early payment, a letter confirming reliable payment. Understanding interests opens solutions that positions block.

A **concession** is something one side gives up in order to move towards agreement. **Never give a concession for nothing.** Link it: 'If you do X, we will do Y.' Concede slowly, in smaller steps, and keep a record. A concession given too quickly encourages more demands.

The **first offer** often matters a great deal because it **anchors** the talks: later offers tend to stay close to it. Make your opening position well supported by evidence (your should-cost estimate), not wildly unreasonable.

head: Tactic
What the supplier does
Good response
rows: 'This price is good only until 5 p.m. today'
Do not be rushed; check the offer properly; say the team needs time to verify it
Test it: ask what is fixed and why; explore other terms
Stay calm, take a break, refocus on the agenda
Claims another buyer pays more or a rival offered less
Do not be drawn; ask for evidence; do not copy by lying yourself
At the end, asks for a small extra such as free delivery
Ask for something in return or decline; the deal is not a bag of extras
A new senior person says earlier points are not binding
Refer to the agreed record and agree to confirm before moving on

blocks.p: **Dishonesty is not an option**: telling a supplier that another firm has offered a lower price when it has not is dishonest and breaks integrity rules. It may also lead to a challenge to the award.

When talks stall (for example on the price of maintenance), try to **reframe**: instead of arguing about the number, propose a fixed fee for set service levels, or split the issue into parts. Other ways: take a break, move to another topic, bring a more senior person, or agree a pilot. If the gap cannot be closed within your limits, use your best alternative.

A public officer is **firm, polite and honest, within her authority**. She listens more than she speaks, keeps notes, stays courteous even when the supplier does not, and never commits beyond her delegation.

sections.title: Non-price terms and wider policy aims

blocks.p: The best terms protect the body after the contract is signed. Negotiate them as carefully as the price.

head: Term
What it does
Example
rows: Sets agreed, measurable standards and the remedies if they are missed
Response within 4 hours; 99.5% system availability each month; monthly report
A fixed sum the supplier pays for each day or week of late delivery
J$50,000 for each week of delay
Moves the price by a published index when costs change, so risk is shared fairly
Fuel price linked to a published index in a five-year fuel supply contract
The supplier repairs or replaces faulty work for an agreed period
Money or a guarantee the body can claim if the supplier fails
A bank guarantee for a percentage of the contract value
When and on what conditions the body pays
Payment on delivery or acceptance; early-payment discount
Allows the body to end the contract for serious failure and to move to another supplier
Hand-over of data and training for the new supplier

blocks.h: Matching the term to the risk

ul: Cleaning for a public hospital: **service levels with measures and remedies** protect quality.
Equipment delivered late: **a clause with agreed deductions per week late** gives a remedy.
Fuel price swings: **a price adjustment linked to a published index**.
Complex ICT: SLA, security, data return and exit terms.

blocks.p: Government policy encourages public bodies to consider wider aims, such as supporting local jobs or reducing waste. These must be raised **in the tender criteria first** and then in talks only as the rules allow. Raising a new aim for the first time after award may be unfair to other bidders.

Match the **risk to the party best able to manage it**: the supplier controls delivery quality; the body controls timely payment and clear requirements. A contract that puts every risk on one side is fragile.

blocks.note: A strong clause that cannot be measured is of no use. For each service level, agree how it is measured, who reports, how often and what happens when the target is missed.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Closing, records and managing the supplier

blocks.p: Near the end of a session, the lead negotiator should **summarise what has been agreed**, to confirm that both sides understand the same terms. Do not leave points vague. After the talks:

flow: Write up the agreed points in clear terms
Confirm them with the supplier in writing
Check the figures twice and test them against the plan and the budget
Get internal approval from the person with authority and any required legal review
Prepare the contract and have it signed by an officer with authority for that value
File the full record of the negotiation

blocks.p: A public body must **keep a full record** of a procurement negotiation, so that the process can be audited and shown to be fair. The record includes the plan, the declarations, the notes of each meeting (offers, concessions, agreements), the approvals and the final terms.
Strategic suppliers should be managed as **long-term relationships** after the contract is signed, to improve results and manage risks together. In practice:

ul: Name a **contract manager** on the body's side.
Hold **regular reviews** against the service levels and costs.
Resolve problems early through the escalation steps in the contract.
Record performance, which will be the evidence at renewal.
Treat the supplier fairly and pay on time, as agreed.

blocks.p: After a major negotiation, hold a **debrief** to record lessons for future negotiations: what worked, what did not, what the supplier did that surprised you, how accurate the should-cost estimate was, and what to change in the template and the team.

blocks.note: Confidentiality continues after the talks. A colleague outside the team who asks for the agency's maximum price should be refused politely: it is kept within the team and, once the contract is signed, in the file.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: explain strategic procurement and why public bodies negotiate within the procurement rules.
state the aim of the procurement rules: value for money through fair, open buying.
explain when a public body may talk with a preferred bidder, and when it should re-tender.
apply probity: conflicts, gifts, confidentiality, honesty, equal treatment.
place a purchase on the Kraljic matrix and choose the matching approach.
judge supplier power from the market.
work out total cost of ownership and compare suppliers over the same period.
write a negotiation plan with aims, priorities, target, walk-away point, concessions, roles and agenda.
name and organise a negotiating team and agree authority limits.
work discounts, percentage reductions, savings against budget, early-payment and warranty sums.
explore interests, make and trade concessions and use the opening offer well.
respond calmly to deadline, take-it-or-leave-it, anger, nibbling and bluff tactics.
negotiate SLAs, liquidated damages, price adjustment, warranty and exit terms.
summarise, record, confirm and obtain approval before the contract is signed.
manage the supplier relationship and hold a debrief.

terms: Strategic procurement
Buying that is high in value or impact, long term and hard to replace.
Preferred bidder
The bidder ranked first after evaluation, with whom final talks may be held where the rules allow.
Probity
Honest, fair and open conduct that stands up to scrutiny.
Delegation
Formal authority to commit the body up to a stated value.
Kraljic matrix
A matrix of cost/impact and supply risk: routine, leverage, bottleneck, strategic.
Bargaining power
The strength a buyer or seller has from its choices and alternatives.
Total cost of ownership
The full cost of an item over its life: price, running, maintenance and disposal.
Should-cost estimate
The buyer's estimate of a fair cost, built up by parts.
Walk-away point
The worst deal the team will accept.
Concession
Something one side gives up to move towards agreement.
Anchor
A first offer that influences later offers.
Service level agreement (SLA)
Agreed measurable standards of service and the remedies for missing them.
Liquidated damages
A fixed sum payable for each day or week of late delivery.
Strategic supplier
A supplier on whom the body depends heavily, managed as a long-term relationship.
Debrief
A review after the negotiation to record lessons.

c1.title: Managed printers for a ministry
c1.text: A ministry in Kingston wants to buy 20 high-volume printers for its head office, to be used for four years. Supplier P offers J$450,000 per printer, with maintenance of J$60,000 and toner of J$90,000 per printer per year. Supplier Q offers J$380,000 per printer, with maintenance of J$85,000 and toner of J$110,000 per printer per year. Many firms in Jamaica supply and service this type of printer. The procurement officer, Mrs Sandra Lawrence, must brief the negotiating team.

c2.title: Diagnostic equipment for a regional hospital
c2.text: A regional hospital will sign a five-year supply and service contract for laboratory diagnostic equipment. Only two firms in Jamaica can service the model required. The budget is J$72 million. The preferred bidder's offer is J$80 million. The second-ranked bidder offered J$76 million. The hospital's team is led by the chief finance officer, Mr Garfield Reid, who has authority to agree up to the budget; anything above needs the board's approval.

c3.title: School desks for the Ministry of Education
c3.text: The ministry negotiates with the preferred bidder for 3,000 desk and chair sets at J$14,000 per set, to be delivered to schools in 14 parishes. The supplier proposes (a) a 5% discount if the ministry orders 3,600 sets instead of 3,000, and (b) a 40% advance payment, whereas the ministry's rules pay on delivery. Near the end of the meeting, the supplier also asks for the ministry to pay the cost of delivery to the schools, which was included in the tender price.

c4.title: Probity during a procurement
c4.text: A public health authority is negotiating a three-year medical supplies contract. A team member, Kerry-Ann, mentions to the lead negotiator that her cousin is a sales manager at the preferred bidder. The supplier then invites the whole team to a site visit followed by lunch at a resort, at the supplier's expense. A former colleague of the lead negotiator who now works for another bidder phones her with the second-ranked bidder's price.

c5.title: Hosting of a ministry's records system
c5.text: A ministry is negotiating a four-year contract with a firm to host its electronic records system. The monthly fee is J$900,000. The ministry wants 99.5% availability each month, measured over a 30-day month (720 hours). The team proposes a service credit of 5% of the monthly fee when the target is missed. The lead negotiator, Ms Rhonda Clarke, also wants the contract to allow the ministry to end it for repeated failure and to recover its data. The permanent secretary has delegated authority to sign contracts up to J$60 million.

questions.q: Which statement about the two offers is correct?
o: Q has the lower purchase price, but P has the lower total cost over four years
P has both the lower purchase price and the lower total cost over four years
Q has the lower purchase price and also the lower total cost over four years
The two offers have the same total cost once toner is left out
questions.why: Q is J$70,000 cheaper to buy, but its yearly maintenance and toner are J$45,000 higher. Over four years P costs J$1,050,000 per printer and Q J$1,160,000.

questions.q: Over four years, how much cheaper are 20 printers from the cheaper supplier on total cost of ownership?
questions.why: P costs J$110,000 less per printer (1,160,000 - 1,050,000). 20 x 110,000 = J$2,200,000. Q has the lower purchase price, but P has the lower total cost.

questions.q: Where does the purchase of the printers most likely sit on the Kraljic matrix, and what approach fits?
o: Leverage, because many suppliers exist, so use competition to get good value
Strategic, because it is a large amount, so build a single long-term supplier
Bottleneck, because printers are scarce, so stockpile them
Routine, because printers are cheap, so spend no time on it
questions.why: The spend is significant but many firms can supply and service printers, so supply risk is low: leverage. Use competition and compare total cost.

questions.q: Supplier Q's lower purchase price is shown to the team. What should Mrs Lawrence tell them about price?
o: Compare total cost over the four years, not the purchase price alone
Choose the lowest purchase price, as running costs are the supplier's concern
Ignore maintenance and toner, because they are paid from a different budget line
Pick the supplier with the highest total, which shows the best quality
questions.why: The cheapest price at purchase is not always the cheapest overall. Total cost of ownership brings in maintenance and toner over the contract life.

questions.q: What percentage reduction from the preferred bidder's offer is needed to reach the budget?
questions.why: (80 - 72) / 80 = 8 / 80 = 0.10, or 10%. 12.5% is 8 as a percentage of the budget, the wrong base.

questions.q: Which walk-away point best fits the hospital's position?
o: No higher than J$76 million, unless the board approves a clear value case
J$80 million, as the preferred bidder has already been ranked first overall
J$85 million, so that there is room left for extras added later in the contract
J$72 million exactly, whatever happens to the talks with the preferred bidder
questions.why: A walk-away point should not be worse than the best alternative (the second-ranked offer of J$76 million) and must respect authority: anything above the budget needs the board's approval.

questions.q: The talks end at J$75 million. What is the reduction as a percentage of the first offer?
questions.why: (80 - 75) / 80 = 5 / 80 = 0.0625, or 6.25%. The base is the first offer. The agreed price is above the budget, so the lead needs the board's approval before agreeing.

questions.q: Only two firms can service the equipment. What does this mean for the team's preparation?
o: Supplier power is high, so prepare an alternative and avoid showing urgency
The hospital has strong bargaining power and can demand whatever it wishes
Negotiation is unnecessary, as the supplier must accept the budget figure
The hospital should reveal its maximum price at the start to speed things up
questions.why: With few suppliers and costly switching, the supplier is in a strong position. The team prepares a best alternative, protects its limits and avoids revealing urgency.

questions.q: What is the discounted price per set if the 5% discount applies?
Compare 3,600 sets at the discounted price with 3,000 sets at J$14,000. What do the 600 extra sets effectively cost each?
What should the ministry consider before accepting the larger order?
o: Whether it needs and can afford the extra sets, and whether the rules allow the change
Whether the supplier would give a bigger discount for an order of any size at all
Whether the extra sets could be sold to private schools to make a profit
Nothing, because a discount offered by a supplier is always worth taking
questions.why: A discount linked to a condition must be tested: is there a real need, is it within the budget, and does a large change in quantity affect fairness to other bidders and the rules?

questions.q: The supplier asks for a 40% advance payment. What is the best response?
o: Ask why it needs the cash, then explore staged payments or a bank guarantee
Agree to it, because suppliers always need cash up front to start work
Refuse to discuss any change to payment terms, whatever the reason given
Accept half of the request without asking for anything in return
questions.why: Explore the interest behind the position. Staged payments tied to delivery or a guarantee protect public money while meeting the supplier's cash-flow need.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann's cousin works for the preferred bidder. What should happen?
o: She declares the interest and stands down from the team's work on this tender
She stays on the team and says nothing, as her cousin is not the owner of the firm
She stays on the team but stays silent whenever the cousin's firm is discussed
She stays on the team and tells her cousin which points the team will raise
questions.why: A private interest that could influence, or appear to influence, the result must be declared. The usual step is to stand down, and the declaration is recorded.

questions.q: How should the team respond to the supplier's lunch invitation at the resort?
o: Decline, record the offer, and have the authority pay for any necessary site visit
Accept, provided that every member of the team attends together
Accept the site visit but not the lunch, and tell nobody about the invitation
Accept the invitation and later give the supplier a better score
questions.why: Hospitality from a bidder during a procurement can look like influence. Decline and record it; if a site visit is needed, the authority should bear its own costs.

questions.q: The former colleague tells the lead negotiator the second-ranked bidder's price. What should she do?
o: Refuse to use it, end the call and report it to the procurement officer
Use it quietly to put pressure on the preferred bidder at the next meeting
Pass the price straight to the preferred bidder so that it can respond
Write it down and keep it ready for use at a later meeting
questions.why: Other bids are confidential. Using leaked information breaks probity and could void the process. Do not use it and report it.

questions.q: Why should the declarations, the invitation and the phone call be recorded in the file?
o: So the process can be audited and shown to have been fair
So the supplier can be told who made the declarations
So the file is longer than competitors' files
So that the lead negotiator is protected from any decision she takes
questions.why: Full records let auditors and reviewers see that conflicts were handled and that the award was not influenced.

questions.q: How many hours of downtime does the 99.5% target allow in a 30-day month?
o: 3.6 hours
36 hours
0.5 hours
7.2 hours

questions.q: What is the service credit if the target is missed, under the proposal of 5% of the monthly fee?
Which term best protects the ministry if the firm repeatedly fails to meet the service levels?
o: A right to end the contract for repeated failure, with data return and hand-over help
A clause that renews the contract automatically for another year after each failure
A promise from the firm that it will do its best to improve in future
A clause that lets the firm raise its monthly fee after any failure
questions.why: Termination and exit terms give the body a real remedy and let it move to another provider without losing its data.

questions.q: The total contract value is J$43.2 million (48 x J$900,000). Who may sign it, and when?
o: An officer with delegated authority for that value, after the terms are confirmed and approved
Ms Clarke alone, as soon as the talks end and the figures look right
The firm's representative, on behalf of both parties to the contract
Any team member who attended every meeting of the negotiation
questions.why: 48 x 900,000 = J$43.2 million, within the permanent secretary's J$60 million delegation. The agreed terms must be confirmed and approved before an authorised officer signs.
